screens.title: Azure Monitor Metrics: The Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Monitor metrics are the bedrock of effective cloud monitoring, providing numerical values that capture a specific aspect of an Azure resource at a given moment. Unlike logs, which offer detailed event records, metrics are lightweight, collected at regular intervals—often every minute—and stored efficiently in a time-series database. This design makes them ideal for near real-time performance monitoring, identifying trends, and setting up alerts for anomalies. For example, a Virtual Machine's C P U utilization, a Storage Account's ingress and egress, or a Web App's HTTP response times are all common platform metrics. These metrics are automatically emitted by Azure resources, giving you immediate visibility into their operational state. Understanding this fundamental difference between metrics and logs is crucial, as each serves a distinct but complementary role in your monitoring strategy. Metrics tell you 'what' is happening quantitatively, while logs explain 'why' it's happening with detailed event information. Azure Monitor Metrics: The Foundation means metrics are lightweight, time-series data for real-time performance; logs provide detailed event information.. In practical terms, quantitative insights into resource health and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Metrics Fundamentals
Core Concept

Azure Monitor Metrics: The Foundation

Quantitative insights into resource health and performance

What are Metrics?

Numerical values representing a specific aspect of an Azure resource at a particular time. They are lightweight and collected at regular intervals.

Key Characteristics

  • Numerical: Always a quantity or percentage.
  • Time-Series: Stored with a timestamp, ideal for trending.
  • Lightweight: Efficient for near real-time monitoring.
  • Proactive: Excellent for spotting anomalies and degradation.
Key Takeaway

Metrics provide quantitative summaries for quick performance insights, complementing detailed event logs for comprehensive monitoring.

Metrics vs. Logs: A Quick Comparison

Metrics

Quantitative summary, time-series, for trending & alerting.

  • CPU %
  • Network I/O
  • Disk IOPS

Logs

Detailed event information, for auditing & troubleshooting.

  • Error messages
  • Access records
  • Application traces

Metrics tell you what is happening; Logs tell you why.

screens.title: Platform Metrics and Their Dimensions
screens.narratorSegment: Every Azure resource, from Virtual Machines to Storage Accounts and Web Apps, automatically emits a comprehensive set of platform metrics. These are the built-in metrics that Azure provides by default, covering essential aspects of resource performance and health. For instance, a Virtual Machine will emit metrics like 'Percentage C P U', 'Network In Total', and 'Disk Read Operations/Sec'. What makes these metrics incredibly powerful are their dimensions. Dimensions are key-value pairs that provide additional context to a metric, allowing for much more granular analysis. Imagine a 'network inbound bytes' metric for a Virtual Machine. Without dimensions, you'd see total traffic. But with a 'NicName' dimension, you can break down that traffic by individual network interface, helping you pinpoint if a specific network adapter is experiencing high load. This ability to slice and dice your metric data using dimensions is fundamental for effective troubleshooting and performance optimization. It allows you to move from a high-level overview to a detailed component-level view, which is essential for diagnosing complex issues. In practical terms, understanding the rich data emitted by azure resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Introducing Metrics Explorer
screens.narratorSegment: The primary tool for interacting with and visualizing metrics in Azure Monitor is the Metrics Explorer, a powerful interface directly accessible within the Azure portal. Think of it as your dashboard for all things performance. To get started, you simply navigate to the Azure resource you wish to monitor—for example, a Virtual Machine. In the left-hand menu, under the 'Monitoring' section, you'll find and select 'Metrics'. This action opens the Metrics Explorer, where you'll first define the scope, which is typically the resource you're currently viewing. Next, you choose the metric namespace, a logical grouping of metrics like 'Virtual Machine Host Metrics'. Finally, you select the specific metric you want to analyze, such as 'Percentage C P U'. Once selected, Metrics Explorer automatically renders a time-series chart, displaying the metric's values over a chosen time range. You can easily adjust this range, from the last 30 minutes to the last 30 days, or even define a custom period, providing immediate and historical insights into your resource's performance. This intuitive visualization is your first step in understanding and diagnosing resource behavior.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Metrics Explorer
Tooling

Introducing Metrics Explorer

Your gateway to visualizing Azure resource performance

What is Metrics Explorer?

The primary tool in the Azure portal for visualizing and analyzing Azure Monitor metrics. It provides an interactive charting experience.

Key Features

  • Scope Selection: Choose the resource to monitor.
  • Metric Namespace: Grouping of related metrics.
  • Metric Selection: Pick the specific data point.
  • Time Range: Adjust view from minutes to months.
Key Takeaway

Metrics Explorer is the central hub for visualizing Azure resource performance, offering flexible charting and time-range adjustments.

Steps to Visualize Metrics

1.Navigate to Azure Resource
2.Select 'Metrics' under Monitoring
3.Choose Metric Namespace & Metric
4.View & Adjust Time-Series Chart

screens.title: Aggregating Metrics: Summarizing Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond basic visualization, Metrics Explorer offers powerful capabilities for deeper analysis, starting with aggregation. Aggregation allows you to combine multiple metric data points over a specified time period into a single, summary value. This is incredibly useful for understanding overall trends rather than just individual data points. Common aggregation types include 'Average' (Avg), which gives you the mean value over the period, 'Minimum' (Min) and 'Maximum' (Max), which show the lowest and highest values, 'Sum' (total), and 'Count' (number of data points). For example, if you're monitoring C P U utilization, viewing the 'Average' C P U over an hour can tell you about the typical workload, while looking at the 'Maximum' C P U during that same hour can highlight peak demands or potential bottlenecks. Choosing the right aggregation type is crucial for accurate interpretation. Using 'Sum' for a percentage metric like C P U across multiple instances, for example, would give a misleadingly high number, whereas 'Average' or 'Maximum' would be more appropriate to understand the load per instance. Always consider what the metric represents and what summary makes the most sense for your analysis.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Aggregating Metrics
Analysis Technique

Aggregating Metrics: Summarizing Performance

Combining data points to reveal trends and overall health

What is Aggregation?

The process of combining multiple metric data points over a time period into a single, summary value. This helps in understanding overall trends.

Common Aggregation Types

  • Avg: Average value over the period.
  • Min/Max: Lowest/Highest value observed.
  • Sum: Total of all values (e.g., total bytes).
  • Count: Number of data points collected.
Key Takeaway

Choose the correct aggregation type (Avg, Max, Sum) based on the metric's nature to avoid misinterpreting performance data.

screens.title: Splitting Metrics by Dimensions for Granular View
screens.narratorSegment: Another critical feature in Metrics Explorer for deeper analysis is 'splitting by dimensions'. If a metric has dimensions, such as 'Instance' for a Virtual Machine Scale Set or 'OperationName' for a Storage Account, you can use the splitting feature to display individual lines on your chart for each unique value of that dimension. This transforms a single, aggregated line into multiple distinct lines, each representing a specific component or aspect. For example, if you're monitoring a Virtual Machine Scale Set and select the 'Percentage C P U' metric, applying splitting by the 'Instance' dimension will show you a separate C P U utilization line for each individual VM instance within that scale set. This is incredibly powerful for identifying if a performance issue is localized to a specific instance or operation, rather than affecting the entire resource uniformly. Without splitting, you might only see an overall high C P U, but with it, you can pinpoint the exact problematic instance, saving significant troubleshooting time. It helps you move from a general observation to a precise diagnosis, making your monitoring efforts much more efficient and targeted.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Splitting Metrics
Analysis Technique

Splitting Metrics: Pinpointing Specific Issues

Breaking down data by dimensions for detailed component analysis

What is Splitting?

Displaying separate lines on a metric chart for each unique value of a selected dimension. This provides a granular view of performance across components.

Why Use Splitting?

  • Localized Issues: Identify if a problem affects one instance or all.
  • Component Comparison: Compare performance across different parts.
  • Targeted Troubleshooting: Focus efforts on specific problematic areas.
Key Takeaway

Splitting metrics by dimensions is essential for diagnosing localized performance issues within a resource, like a single VM in a scale set.

Before vs. After Splitting (VMSS CPU)

Before Splitting

Overall VMSS CPU %

CPU %
Time

A single line showing combined CPU, hiding individual instance behavior.

After Splitting

VMSS CPU % by Instance

Splitting helps identify if a problem is widespread or isolated to specific components.

screens.title: Filtering Metrics: Focusing Your Investigation
screens.narratorSegment: Complementing aggregation and splitting, filtering by dimensions is another powerful technique in Metrics Explorer that allows you to narrow down your data to specific dimension values. While splitting shows you all values of a dimension, filtering lets you select only the ones you're interested in, effectively focusing your analysis. For example, if you have a Virtual Machine with multiple disks, and you're looking at the 'Disk Read Operations/Sec' metric, you might want to investigate the performance of a particular disk. By applying a filter on the 'LUN' dimension and selecting a specific Logical Unit Number, you can isolate the data for just that disk. This is incredibly useful when you already suspect an issue with a particular component or want to exclude irrelevant data from your view. Filtering can be used in conjunction with splitting, allowing you to first split by a dimension to see all components, and then filter to focus on a subset of those components. This combination provides a highly targeted and efficient way to analyze your metric data, helping you quickly hone in on the root cause of performance issues.

Analysis Technique

Filtering Metrics: Focusing Your Investigation

Narrowing down data to specific dimension values

What is Filtering?

The process of narrowing down metric data to specific dimension values, allowing you to focus your analysis on particular components or operations.

When to Use Filtering

  • Isolate Components: View data for a specific disk, network interface, or instance.
  • Exclude Noise: Remove irrelevant data points from your chart.
  • Combine with Splitting: Refine a split view to focus on a subset of components.
Key Takeaway

Filtering allows precise control over which metric data is displayed, enabling highly targeted analysis and troubleshooting.

screens.title: Diagnosing VMSS CPU Spikes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical scenario to see how these analysis techniques come together. Imagine you're monitoring a Virtual Machine Scale Set, or VMSS, and you notice that the overall 'Percentage C P U' metric is occasionally spiking. Your goal is to determine if this spike is affecting all instances equally or just a few. In Metrics Explorer, you would first select your VMSS as the scope and choose the 'Percentage C P U' metric. Initially, you might see a single line representing the aggregated C P U across all instances. To get to the root cause, you would then 'Apply splitting' by the 'Instance' dimension. This action transforms your chart, displaying a separate line for each individual VM instance within the scale set. If you observe that only one or two instances are experiencing high C P U while the others remain normal, it immediately points you to investigate those specific instances. Perhaps a misbehaving application or a specific workload is causing the issue. Conversely, if all instances show high C P U, it suggests a broader problem, such as an overall increase in demand, indicating that your scale set might need to scale out. This targeted analysis significantly reduces troubleshooting time and helps you make informed decisions about your infrastructure.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›VMSS CPU Diagnosis

Diagnosing VMSS CPU Spikes

screens.title: Best Practices: Avoiding Metric Misinterpretations
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Azure Monitor metrics, it's crucial to be aware of common pitfalls that can lead to misinterpretations and incorrect diagnostic decisions. One of the most frequent mistakes is misinterpreting the aggregation type. For instance, if you're monitoring the 'Percentage C P U' across multiple instances in a Virtual Machine Scale Set, using 'Sum' as the aggregation type would give you a total C P U percentage that could easily exceed 100%, leading to a misleadingly high number. In such a scenario, 'Average' or 'Maximum' would typically be more appropriate to understand the load per instance or the peak load experienced by any single instance. Always consider what the metric truly represents and what aggregation method makes logical sense for your analysis. Another best practice is to always compare current performance against a baseline. What looks like a spike might be normal behavior during peak hours. Also, ensure your time ranges are appropriate for the trend you're trying to identify. Short ranges for real-time, longer ranges for historical trends. By carefully selecting aggregation types, understanding your metrics, and establishing baselines, you can ensure your analysis is accurate and actionable, preventing unnecessary troubleshooting or incorrect scaling decisions.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Avoiding Mistakes
Best Practices

Best Practices: Avoiding Metric Misinterpretations

Ensuring accurate analysis and preventing misleading conclusions

Common Mistake: Wrong Aggregation

Using 'Sum' for percentage-based metrics (like CPU %) across multiple instances can lead to misleadingly high values. Always choose an aggregation that makes logical sense for the metric.

Other Best Practices

  • Establish Baselines: Understand normal performance.
  • Appropriate Time Ranges: Match range to analysis goal.
  • Combine with Logs: Use metrics for 'what', logs for 'why'.
Key Takeaway

Always align your aggregation choice with the metric's nature and establish baselines to avoid misinterpreting performance data.

Aggregation Choices: CPU Percentage Example

Incorrect: Sum

For CPU % across 3 VMs (e.g., 50%, 60%, 70%)

180%

Misleadingly high, doesn't represent individual VM load.

Correct: Avg or Max

For CPU % across 3 VMs (e.g., 50%, 60%, 70%)

Avg: 60%

Accurately reflects typical load per instance.

Always choose aggregation that aligns with the metric's meaning to avoid false alarms or missed issues.

Welcome to this crucial chapter on collecting and analyzing metrics with Azure Monitor. In today's cloud environments, understanding the performance and health of your resources is paramount. Metrics provide the quantitative data you need, offering numerical values that represent specific aspects of your Azure resources at any given time. Think of them as the vital signs of your cloud infrastructure and applications. This chapter will equip you with the skills to not only access these metrics but also to interpret them effectively, using powerful tools like Metrics Explorer. By the end, you'll be able to identify performance trends, diagnose issues, and even extend monitoring to your custom application data, ensuring your Azure solutions run optimally and reliably. Let's dive in and discover how to transform raw data into actionable insights.

By the end of this chapter, you'll gain a solid understanding of how Azure Monitor metrics function and how to leverage them effectively. Our first set of objectives focuses on foundational knowledge and practical visualization. You'll learn to identify the various types of metrics Azure resources emit and understand their underlying structure, which is crucial for interpreting the data correctly. We'll then move into hands-on application, showing you how to utilize the powerful Metrics Explorer in the Azure portal to visualize your resource's performance in real-time. This will empower you to quickly grasp the current state and historical trends of your Azure environment, setting the stage for more advanced analysis. These skills are fundamental for any Azure administrator looking to maintain a healthy and responsive cloud infrastructure. Learning Objectives means mastering azure monitor metrics is crucial for maintaining healthy, high-performing azure environments.. In practical terms, what you'll achieve in this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building on our initial objectives, this screen outlines the advanced skills you'll acquire to truly master Azure Monitor metrics. We'll explore the concept of custom metrics, understanding why they are essential for monitoring application-specific data that Azure's platform metrics might not cover. This capability extends your monitoring reach beyond infrastructure into the heart of your applications. Furthermore, you'll learn to diagnose complex performance issues by applying a combination of metric analysis techniques, moving beyond simple observation to active problem-solving. We'll also highlight the importance of distinguishing between appropriate aggregation types, a common pitfall that can lead to misinterpretations. Finally, you'll gain the knowledge to integrate custom metrics seamlessly, providing a comprehensive, end-to-end view of your entire Azure solution. These objectives will transform you into a highly effective Azure monitoring professional.

Azure Monitor metrics are the bedrock of effective cloud monitoring, providing numerical values that capture a specific aspect of an Azure resource at a given moment. Unlike logs, which offer detailed event records, metrics are lightweight, collected at regular intervals—often every minute—and stored efficiently in a time-series database. This design makes them ideal for near real-time performance monitoring, identifying trends, and setting up alerts for anomalies. For example, a Virtual Machine's C P U utilization, a Storage Account's ingress and egress, or a Web App's HTTP response times are all common platform metrics. These metrics are automatically emitted by Azure resources, giving you immediate visibility into their operational state. Understanding this fundamental difference between metrics and logs is crucial, as each serves a distinct but complementary role in your monitoring strategy. Metrics tell you 'what' is happening quantitatively, while logs explain 'why' it's happening with detailed event information. Azure Monitor Metrics: The Foundation means metrics are lightweight, time-series data for real-time performance; logs provide detailed event information.. In practical terms, quantitative insights into resource health and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Every Azure resource, from Virtual Machines to Storage Accounts and Web Apps, automatically emits a comprehensive set of platform metrics. These are the built-in metrics that Azure provides by default, covering essential aspects of resource performance and health. For instance, a Virtual Machine will emit metrics like 'Percentage C P U', 'Network In Total', and 'Disk Read Operations/Sec'. What makes these metrics incredibly powerful are their dimensions. Dimensions are key-value pairs that provide additional context to a metric, allowing for much more granular analysis. Imagine a 'network inbound bytes' metric for a Virtual Machine. Without dimensions, you'd see total traffic. But with a 'NicName' dimension, you can break down that traffic by individual network interface, helping you pinpoint if a specific network adapter is experiencing high load. This ability to slice and dice your metric data using dimensions is fundamental for effective troubleshooting and performance optimization. It allows you to move from a high-level overview to a detailed component-level view, which is essential for diagnosing complex issues. The primary tool for interacting with and visualizing metrics in Azure Monitor is the Metrics Explorer, a powerful interface directly accessible within the Azure portal. Think of it as your dashboard for all things performance. To get started, you simply navigate to the Azure resource you wish to monitor—for example, a Virtual Machine. In the left-hand menu, under the 'Monitoring' section, you'll find and select 'Metrics'. This action opens the Metrics Explorer, where you'll first define the scope, which is typically the resource you're currently viewing. Next, you choose the metric namespace, a logical grouping of metrics like 'Virtual Machine Host Metrics'. Finally, you select the specific metric you want to analyze, such as 'Percentage C P U'. Once selected, Metrics Explorer automatically renders a time-series chart, displaying the metric's values over a chosen time range. You can easily adjust this range, from the last 30 minutes to the last 30 days, or even define a custom period, providing immediate and historical insights into your resource's performance. This intuitive visualization is your first step in understanding and diagnosing resource behavior.

Beyond basic visualization, Metrics Explorer offers powerful capabilities for deeper analysis, starting with aggregation. Aggregation allows you to combine multiple metric data points over a specified time period into a single, summary value. This is incredibly useful for understanding overall trends rather than just individual data points. Common aggregation types include 'Average' (Avg), which gives you the mean value over the period, 'Minimum' (Min) and 'Maximum' (Max), which show the lowest and highest values, 'Sum' (total), and 'Count' (number of data points). For example, if you're monitoring C P U utilization, viewing the 'Average' C P U over an hour can tell you about the typical workload, while looking at the 'Maximum' C P U during that same hour can highlight peak demands or potential bottlenecks. Choosing the right aggregation type is crucial for accurate interpretation. Using 'Sum' for a percentage metric like C P U across multiple instances, for example, would give a misleadingly high number, whereas 'Average' or 'Maximum' would be more appropriate to understand the load per instance. Always consider what the metric represents and what summary makes the most sense for your analysis.

Another critical feature in Metrics Explorer for deeper analysis is 'splitting by dimensions'. If a metric has dimensions, such as 'Instance' for a Virtual Machine Scale Set or 'OperationName' for a Storage Account, you can use the splitting feature to display individual lines on your chart for each unique value of that dimension. This transforms a single, aggregated line into multiple distinct lines, each representing a specific component or aspect. For example, if you're monitoring a Virtual Machine Scale Set and select the 'Percentage C P U' metric, applying splitting by the 'Instance' dimension will show you a separate C P U utilization line for each individual VM instance within that scale set. This is incredibly powerful for identifying if a performance issue is localized to a specific instance or operation, rather than affecting the entire resource uniformly. Without splitting, you might only see an overall high C P U, but with it, you can pinpoint the exact problematic instance, saving significant troubleshooting time. It helps you move from a general observation to a precise diagnosis, making your monitoring efforts much more efficient and targeted.

Complementing aggregation and splitting, filtering by dimensions is another powerful technique in Metrics Explorer that allows you to narrow down your data to specific dimension values. While splitting shows you all values of a dimension, filtering lets you select only the ones you're interested in, effectively focusing your analysis. For example, if you have a Virtual Machine with multiple disks, and you're looking at the 'Disk Read Operations/Sec' metric, you might want to investigate the performance of a particular disk. By applying a filter on the 'LUN' dimension and selecting a specific Logical Unit Number, you can isolate the data for just that disk. This is incredibly useful when you already suspect an issue with a particular component or want to exclude irrelevant data from your view. Filtering can be used in conjunction with splitting, allowing you to first split by a dimension to see all components, and then filter to focus on a subset of those components. This combination provides a highly targeted and efficient way to analyze your metric data, helping you quickly hone in on the root cause of performance issues.

Let's walk through a practical scenario to see how these analysis techniques come together. Imagine you're monitoring a Virtual Machine Scale Set, or VMSS, and you notice that the overall 'Percentage C P U' metric is occasionally spiking. Your goal is to determine if this spike is affecting all instances equally or just a few. In Metrics Explorer, you would first select your VMSS as the scope and choose the 'Percentage C P U' metric. Initially, you might see a single line representing the aggregated C P U across all instances. To get to the root cause, you would then 'Apply splitting' by the 'Instance' dimension. This action transforms your chart, displaying a separate line for each individual VM instance within the scale set. If you observe that only one or two instances are experiencing high C P U while the others remain normal, it immediately points you to investigate those specific instances. Perhaps a misbehaving application or a specific workload is causing the issue. Conversely, if all instances show high C P U, it suggests a broader problem, such as an overall increase in demand, indicating that your scale set might need to scale out. This targeted analysis significantly reduces troubleshooting time and helps you make informed decisions about your infrastructure.
